questions.prompt: At 25°C, what is the pH of neutral pure water?
questions.explanation: At 25°C, neutral water has equal H⁺ and OH⁻ concentrations and pH 7.

questions.prompt: Which solution is acidic at 25°C?
questions.explanation: Acidic aqueous solutions have pH below the neutral value at the stated temperature.

questions.prompt: Universal indicator is green in an approximately neutral solution. What is the likely pH at 25°C?
questions.explanation: Universal indicator provides an approximate colour-based range, not a highly precise pH.

questions.prompt: Why can phenolphthalein be colourless in both pH 2 and pH 7 solutions?
options: Both solutions must be equally concentrated.
Both solutions must be strong acids.
Both are below its visible alkaline transition range.
questions.explanation: A single indicator cannot distinguish every pH below its transition range.

questions.prompt: What colour does blue litmus paper turn in an acidic solution?
options: Blue because acids never affect it
questions.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus red.

questions.prompt: What happens to red litmus paper in an alkaline solution?
options: It turns redder in every case.
questions.explanation: Alkalis turn red litmus blue.

questions.prompt: Why should a fresh sample be used when comparing indicators?
options: Every indicator needs a different chemical identity of sample.
Indicators cannot be used on solutions.
Earlier reagents could contaminate or change the sample.
questions.explanation: Fresh portions keep the comparison fair and avoid mixing indicator reagents.

questions.prompt: What can red-cabbage extract normally tell you?
options: An exact molar concentration for every acid
Whether every solute is a metal
The exact number of molecules in a beaker
An approximate acid–base range from its colour
questions.explanation: Natural indicator colours depend on preparation and conditions and are approximate.

questions.prompt: Two indicators give different colours in the same unchanged sample. Which explanation is best?
options: They have different transition ranges and colours.
The sample must have two different pH values at once.
One colour proves the sample has no ions.
The indicators must have identical chemistry.
questions.explanation: Each indicator responds differently over its own pH interval.

questions.prompt: If [H⁺] increases tenfold in an ideal dilute solution, what happens to pH?
questions.explanation: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺], so a tenfold increase lowers pH by one unit.

questions.prompt: What does a strong acid do in a dilute aqueous solution?
options: It must have a high concentration.
questions.explanation: Strength describes the extent of ionisation, not the amount per volume.

questions.prompt: What does a weak acid establish in water?
options: A permanent precipitate in every solution
An equilibrium with only partial ionisation
questions.explanation: Weak acids partially ionise and have an equilibrium between acid and ions.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly defines concentration?
options: Amount of solute per solution volume
Fraction of acid molecules ionised only
questions.explanation: Concentration is an amount-to-volume ratio.

questions.prompt: Equal-concentration HCl and ethanoic acid solutions are compared at 25°C. Which normally has the lower pH?
options: pH cannot differ at equal concentration
questions.explanation: HCl ionises more completely, giving a higher H⁺ concentration under this comparison.

questions.prompt: What changes when a solution of HCl is diluted with water?
options: Its concentration falls while HCl remains a strong acid.
Strong means it cannot be diluted.
questions.explanation: Dilution changes amount per volume, not the intrinsic acid identity or strength.

questions.prompt: Why is a comparison of pH alone insufficient to rank acid strength without other information?
questions.explanation: Control concentration and conditions when comparing ionisation strength.

questions.prompt: Which is a weak base in water?
options: Sodium hydroxide as a strong-base comparison
Sodium chloride as a neutral-salt comparison
questions.explanation: Ammonia reacts partially with water to form NH₄⁺ and OH⁻.

questions.prompt: Which equation correctly represents ethanoic acid ionisation?
questions.explanation: The reversible arrow represents partial ionisation equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Why may a strong electrolyte conduct better than a weak electrolyte at equal analytical concentration?
options: The word strong guarantees a larger beaker.
It generally provides more mobile ions.
questions.explanation: Ion concentration matters, though ion mobility and temperature also affect conductivity.

questions.prompt: Which statement can be true?
options: Every weak acid is dilute by definition.
Every strong acid is concentrated by definition.
Dilution changes all strong acids into weak acids.
A weak acid can be concentrated and a strong acid dilute.
questions.explanation: Strength and concentration describe different properties.

questions.prompt: 0.02 mol of solute is in 0.2 L of solution. What is its concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Use c = n/V with volume in litres.

questions.prompt: 0.03 mol of solute is in 0.3 L of solution. What is its concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Use c = n/V with volume in litres.

questions.prompt: 0.025 mol of solute is in 0.5 L of solution. What is its concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Use c = n/V with volume in litres.

questions.prompt: 0.1 mol of solute is in 2 L of solution. What is its concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Use c = n/V with volume in litres.

questions.prompt: A dilute water-based solution has 60 mg of solute in 2 L. Assuming density about 1 kg/L, what is its approximate ppm by mass?
questions.explanation: mg/L is approximately ppm by mass for this dilute aqueous density assumption.

questions.prompt: A dilute water-based solution has 20 mg of solute in 4 L. Assuming density about 1 kg/L, what is its approximate ppm by mass?
questions.explanation: mg/L is approximately ppm by mass for this dilute aqueous density assumption.

questions.prompt: A dilute water-based solution has 150 mg of solute in 3 L. Assuming density about 1 kg/L, what is its approximate ppm by mass?
questions.explanation: mg/L is approximately ppm by mass for this dilute aqueous density assumption.

questions.prompt: A 0.200 mol/L solution is diluted from 50.0 mL to 200.0 mL without losing solute. What is the final concentration in mol/L?
A solution contains 80 mg of solute in 2 L. Add 2 L of water. What is its final mass concentration in mg/L?
questions.explanation: The same 80 mg is now in 4 L, giving 20 mg/L.

questions.prompt: Which extra information is needed to convert a mass concentration to molar concentration?
questions.explanation: Divide mass concentration in g/L by molar mass in g/mol.

questions.prompt: What are the products of an acid reacting with an alkali?
questions.explanation: Neutralisation between acid and alkali forms salt and water.

questions.prompt: What salt forms from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid supplies chloride and sodium hydroxide supplies sodium ions.

questions.prompt: What salt forms from nitric acid and potassium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Nitric acid forms nitrates; potassium is the cation.

questions.prompt: What is the formula of the salt from sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: Two K⁺ balance one SO₄²⁻; the full equation uses 2KOH.

questions.prompt: Which net ionic equation describes strong-acid / strong-alkali neutralisation?
questions.explanation: H⁺ and OH⁻ combine to form water; spectator ions are omitted.

questions.prompt: In HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, which ions are spectators?
questions.explanation: Sodium and chloride remain aqueous and unchanged in the net ionic equation.

questions.prompt: Does mixing equal acid and alkali volumes always give equivalence?
options: No; concentration and stoichiometry also matter.
Yes, because every acid has one proton.
No acid can react with an alkali.
questions.explanation: Equal amounts of reacting H⁺ and OH⁻, not equal volumes alone, determine equivalence.

questions.prompt: At 25°C, what is the ideal pH at equivalence for HCl and NaOH?
questions.explanation: A strong acid and strong base form a neutral salt solution in this ideal comparison.

questions.prompt: Which describes the thermal effect of acid–alkali neutralisation?
options: It creates electrical charge from nothing.
questions.explanation: Formation of water from H⁺ and OH⁻ releases heat in the usual dilute strong-acid/base reaction.

questions.prompt: How many moles of NaOH are needed to neutralise 1 mol of H₂SO₄ completely?
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.

questions.prompt: Which gas is produced by magnesium and dilute HCl?
questions.explanation: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

questions.prompt: Which gas is produced by calcium carbonate and dilute HCl?
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with acids to form salt, CO₂ and water.

questions.prompt: Which test identifies carbon dioxide?
options: It gives the characteristic hydrogen pop.
questions.explanation: CO₂ reacts with limewater to form a calcium carbonate precipitate.

questions.prompt: Which test identifies hydrogen?
options: A burning splint gives a pop.
questions.explanation: The pop is a small hydrogen combustion test.

questions.prompt: Which metal does not release H₂ from dilute non-oxidising HCl in this list?
questions.explanation: Copper lies below hydrogen in the relevant school reactivity comparison.

questions.prompt: What salt normally forms from iron and dilute HCl?
questions.explanation: Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂ under these conditions.

questions.prompt: Which balanced equation is correct for Mg and HCl?
questions.explanation: Balance two Cl and two H atoms with 2HCl.

questions.prompt: What products are expected from an acid and a carbonate?
questions.explanation: The carbonate ion is converted into CO₂ and water by acid.

questions.prompt: Equal masses of Mg and Zn react fully with excess acid. Why can their H₂ amounts differ?
options: Equal masses are not equal amounts in moles.
The gas must always have different identities.
Mg and Zn have the same molar mass.
questions.explanation: Different molar masses mean different moles of metal for the same mass.

questions.prompt: Which condition is important when comparing metal reaction rates?
options: Use any different acid and any temperature.
Keep temperature, concentration and surface-area conditions comparable.
questions.explanation: A fair rate comparison controls the factors that affect reaction speed.

questions.prompt: A monoprotic acid sample of 25.0 mL neutralises 20.0 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaOH. What is the acid concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Use the 1:1 mole ratio: c(acid) = c(base) × V(base) / V(acid).

questions.prompt: A monoprotic acid sample of 20.0 mL neutralises 15.0 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaOH. What is the acid concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Use the 1:1 mole ratio: c(acid) = c(base) × V(base) / V(acid).

questions.prompt: A monoprotic acid sample of 25.0 mL neutralises 30.0 mL of 0.1 mol/L NaOH. What is the acid concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Use the 1:1 mole ratio: c(acid) = c(base) × V(base) / V(acid).

questions.prompt: A monoprotic acid sample of 10.0 mL neutralises 12.0 mL of 0.2 mol/L NaOH. What is the acid concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Use the 1:1 mole ratio: c(acid) = c(base) × V(base) / V(acid).

questions.prompt: What does a burette measure in a titration?
questions.explanation: Delivered volume is the final reading minus the initial reading.

questions.prompt: Why use smaller additions near a titration endpoint?
options: The acid stops having any ions.
The indicator becomes a catalyst for gas production.
A small volume change can cause a large pH change there.
questions.explanation: Add dropwise near the endpoint to avoid excess titrant.

questions.prompt: What indicates the chosen phenolphthalein endpoint for diluted vinegar and NaOH?
options: An intense permanent dark pink as the target
questions.explanation: Faint pink marks entry into the indicator transition; deep pink often means overshooting.

questions.prompt: Why can a weak-acid / strong-base equivalence point be above pH 7?
options: The conjugate base reacts with water to produce some OH⁻.
Na⁺ alone creates all the OH⁻.
All acids are neutral before titration.
questions.explanation: Ethanoate hydrolysis makes the equivalence mixture alkaline.

questions.prompt: Why are repeat concordant titres useful?
options: They prove the exact true value without any systematic error.
They remove the need for correct apparatus.
They support precision and help identify inconsistent trials.
questions.explanation: Agreement improves confidence in repeatability, though systematic errors can remain.

questions.prompt: A titration finds 0.0800 mol/L in a vinegar sample that was diluted by a factor of 10. What was the original concentration in mol/L?
questions.explanation: Multiply the diluted concentration by 10: 0.800 mol/L.

questions.prompt: After adding excess CuO to dilute sulfuric acid, why filter?
options: To remove dissolved copper sulfate ions
To turn the salt into a gas
questions.explanation: The desired salt is dissolved; excess solid is the residue.

questions.prompt: How do you recover crystals from the copper sulfate filtrate?
options: Add all the insoluble residue back.
Concentrate gently, then allow it to cool.
Filter the dissolved ions out with ordinary filter paper.
Assume crystals must form without a concentration change.
questions.explanation: Cooling a sufficiently concentrated solution can form crystals.

questions.prompt: Why is adding excess insoluble base useful?
options: It guarantees the final product contains excess dissolved acid.
It removes all spectator ions by itself.
It uses up the acid and the excess can be filtered away.
It converts every salt into an insoluble solid.
questions.explanation: Choose a reactant whose unreacted excess is separable.

questions.prompt: What is the formula of Epsom salt?
questions.explanation: Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate heptahydrate.

questions.prompt: Which family of salts is generally soluble in water?
questions.explanation: Common nitrates are soluble; other families have important exceptions.

questions.prompt: Which pair of aqueous ions forms an insoluble silver chloride precipitate?
questions.explanation: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl(s).

questions.prompt: Which equation represents a barium sulfate precipitate?
questions.explanation: Barium sulfate is an important insoluble sulfate exception.

questions.prompt: After filtering a precipitate, why wash it with distilled water?
options: To dissolve every precipitate completely by definition
To remove soluble impurities from the solid
questions.explanation: Washing removes solution containing soluble spectator ions.

questions.prompt: Which method suits an insoluble salt?
options: Mix soluble ion sources, then filter, wash and dry the precipitate.
Always use titration followed by complete evaporation.
Distil the solid into the filter paper.
questions.explanation: Precipitation makes the insoluble product directly as a filterable solid.

questions.prompt: Where do the waters in a hydrated crystal come from?
options: Water incorporated from the crystallising solution
The filter paper turning into hydrogen
questions.explanation: Water of crystallisation becomes part of the crystal structure during crystallisation.

questions.prompt: What makes an acid–bicarbonate bath-bomb mixture fizz when wet?
options: Oxygen is split from water by a battery.
questions.explanation: Acid reacts with hydrogencarbonate to form CO₂ and water.

questions.prompt: Why can baking powder release CO₂ when water is added?
options: It contains bicarbonate and suitable acid salts.
questions.explanation: Water lets the acid and bicarbonate partners react.

questions.prompt: What is cream of tartar?
options: An acid salt, potassium hydrogen tartrate
questions.explanation: It can supply the acid partner in a raising mixture.

questions.prompt: Why does bicarbonate plus water alone not show the same room-temperature acid fizz?
options: Water always supplies unlimited strong acid.
The required acid partner is missing.
questions.explanation: Strong heating can cause a different decomposition, but that is not this unheated comparison.

questions.prompt: What is a common soap chemically?
options: A sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid
questions.explanation: Soap ions contain a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail.

questions.prompt: How does soap help disperse oil in water?
options: It changes oil molecules into water molecules.
It makes every oil molecularly soluble without interfaces.
It removes all electrical charge from water.
It stabilises oil droplets with water-attracting heads facing outward.
questions.explanation: Soap supports emulsification rather than converting oil into water.

questions.prompt: What is saponification of a fat in this context?
options: Alkaline hydrolysis forming glycerol and fatty-acid salts
questions.explanation: A fat is an ester; alkaline hydrolysis gives soap salts and glycerol.

questions.prompt: Which net ionic equation describes acid reacting with hydrogencarbonate?
questions.explanation: Atoms and charge balance in acid-driven carbon dioxide release.

questions.prompt: Why can two bath-bomb formulations fizz at different rates?
options: Every mixture must have the same rate.
Rate is determined by the colour of the bowl alone.
Particle size, ingredient proportions and conditions affect the rate.
More foam always proves more moles of acid.
questions.explanation: Qualitative appearance is not by itself a quantitative amount or rate measurement.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a soap emulsion is correct?
options: All water molecules become soap ions.
A permanent emulsion must be an element.
Oil is dispersed in droplets; it has not become a true molecular solution.
questions.explanation: Emulsification stabilises a dispersed phase at oil–water interfaces.
